text: Vol:.(1234567890) Journal of Electronic Materials (2022) 51:4772–4779 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11664-022-09751-z 1 3 TOPICAL COLLECTION: ADVANCED METAL ION BATTERIES Protecting Li Metal Anode While Suppressing “Shuttle Effect” of Li‐S Battery Through Localized High‐Concentration Electrolyte Zhenpeng Hou1 · Peng‐Fei Wang2,3 · Xinyi Sun1 · Wei Li1 · Chuanchao Sheng1 · Ping He1 Received: 20 April 2022 / Accepted: 2 June 2022 / Published online: 1 July 2022 © The Minerals, Metals & Materials Society 2022 Abstract Li-S batteries are widely studied due to their superior theoretical energy density.
However, the “shuttle effect” on the cathode and the unstable Li metal anode hinder their practical application.
During cycling, the “shuttle effect” leads to severe self-discharge and accelerates the capacity decay.
Moreover, the shuttled polysulfides aggravate the growth of dendrites and the loss of Li, causing a low Coulombic efficiency.
Considering electrolyte plays a crucial role in the polysulfides solvation behavior and solid electrolyte interphase (SEI)-formation process, a well-designed electrolyte is required.
Here, we report a local high-concentration electrolyte for Li-S batteries.
This electrolyte is prepared by adding “diluent” 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl methyl ether (TME) to the conventional electrolyte.
The reduction of free solvent in the Li-ion solvation sheath suppresses the dissolution of the polysulfides, and more anion-derived SEI can be formed.
Our work simultaneously restrains the “shuttle effect” of the cathode and builds a stable SEI on the anode to protect the Li metal.

Without any ­LiNO3 additive, the average Coulombic efficiency of the Li anode can reach 98.87% after 120 cycles, and Li-S batteries with superior capacity retention of 60% after 400 cycles at 0.5 C can be achieved.
Keywords Local high-concentration electrolyte · Li metal anode · Coulombic efficiency · Shuttle effect · Li-S battery.

Introduction As technology develops, energy storage apparatus has become increasingly important.1 Among them, Li-S batteries are considered as favorable energy storage apparatus because of their superior theoretical specific energy and specific capacity.2 Also, S serves as the cathode material in Li-S batteries, which is abundant and environmentally friendly.3 Unfortunately, there are still some difficulties hindering the feasible utilization of Li-S batteries.4,5 In the cathode, the Li polysulfide (LiPS) will be formed during the cycles, and it will further migrate to the Li metal anode.

The LiPSs will be reduced on the Li metal anode, and subsequently migrate back to the cathode to be oxidized, leading to an overcharge phenomenon (also known as the “shuttle effect”).6 This phenomenon leads to low Coulombic efficiency (CE), severe self-discharge, inferior utilization of sulfur, and rapid capacity decay during the cycles.

Unstable Li metal anodes in Li-S batteries is another problem, although Li metal has been considered to be the ultimate alternate for the Li-battery anode due to the uppermost theoretical specific capacity and the lowermost electrode potential.7 The rapid formation of Li-dendrite and inevitable parasitic reactions with the electrolyte accelerate the failure of the battery.8 To overcome these problems, researchers have developed various methods.

For the cathode, many scientists have demonstrated that the chemisorption of polysulfides by hollow porous carbon,9 metal oxides,10,11 phosphides,12 carbides,13 or nitrides,14 or ­electrocatalysis15 of the reaction process is a valid strategy to suppress the “shuttle effect”.16 Nevertheless, from a thermodynamic point of view, these strategies can only Zhenpeng Hou and Peng-Fei Wang have contributed equally to this work. * Peng‐Fei Wang wangpengfei@neuq.edu.cn 1 Center of Energy Storage Materials & Technology, College of Engineering and Applied Sciences, National Laboratory of Solid State Microstructures, and Collaborative Innovation Center of Advanced Microstructures, Nanjing University, Nanjing 210093, People’s Republic of China 2 School of Materials Science and Engineering, Northeastern University, Shenyang 110819, People’s Republic of China 3 School of Resources and Materials, Northeastern University at Qinhuangdao, Qinhuangdao 066004, People’s Republic of China

Recently, electrolyte design is considered an effective strategy to deal with the “shuttle effect” and also achieve stable Li metal anodes.30 One promising approach is increasing the electrolyte concentration.
Under high concentration, the solubility of Li polysulfides can be evidently reduced, and the shuttle of polysulfides can be suppressed.

This is because, in highconcentration electrolytes, almost all the solvent molecules are coordinated with salt cations, and there is almost no free solvent in the solution, which reduces the dissolution of the polysulfides.

In addition, in high-concentration electrolyte, Li salts are more likely to react with Li metal, forming a tremendously dense and robust solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer rich in inorganic components, which successfully prevent the corrosion of the Li metal.
Nevertheless, high-concentration electrolytes suffer from the hindrances of high viscidity, relatively low ionic conductivity, and expensive Li salts, which limit their commercial applications.
To overcome these problems, a local high-concentration electrolyte (LHCE) has been developed.
By adding a “diluent” which has little or even no solubility for Li salts to the high-concentration electrolyte, 31 the original solvated structure can be retained.
At the same time, it can effectively reduce the total salt concentration of the entire electrolyte system.
Under this structure, low viscosity, high ionic conductivity, and economical electrolytes can be achieved.
In this study, we employ a novel “diluent”, 1, 1, 2, 2-tetrafluoroethyl methyl ether (TME), to design a LHCE system (LiTFSI-DME/DOL-TME).
In this system, the reduction of free solvent in Li-ion solvation sheath effectively inhibits the dissolution of the polysulfides.

Meanwhile, more TFSIderived inorganic layers along with the organic outer layer arising from dimethoxyethane (DME) and dioxolane (DOL) solvent will build a robust SEI layer, which effectively improves the cyclic stability of the Li metal anode.
Our work simultaneously restrains the “shuttle effect” of the sulfur cathode and builds a robust SEI upon the anode to protect the Li metal.
Without using ­LiNO3, a superior average CE of Li-Cu batteries can be achieved, and the capacity retention of Li-S batteries were also evidently improved.

Results and Discussion The CE of Li‐Cu Batteries with Different Electrolytes The Coulombic efficiency of Li-Cu batteries with the LHCE (LiTFSI-DME/DOL-TME) system was evaluated, and the molar ratio of LiTFSI:DME:DOL:TME was 1:1.5:1.5:6 for a total salt concentration equivalent to 1.8 M LiTFSI-DME/ DOL/TME.

For comparison, two other electrolytes were also tested: high-concentration electrolyte (LiTFSI-DME/ DOL, the molar ratio of LiTFSI:DME:DOL is 1:1.5:1.5 for a total salt concentration equivalent to 5.5 M LiTFSI-DME/ DOL) denoted as HCE, and a low-concentration electrolyte (1M LiTFSI-DME/DOL v: v = 1:1) denoted as LCE.
Li-Cu batteries were used to calculate the CE in the three systems (Fig. 1).
The battery using LCE showed a poor initial CE of only 76% (Fig. 1a), and the CE quickly dropped to less than 80% after 40 cycles.
The initial CE of Li was slightly improved to 82% when HCE was used (Fig. 1b).
The CE then further increased to 98.5% (Fig.
S1), while it began to decline after 60 cycles.
Consequently, increasing the concentration of the electrolyte can evidently enhance the reversibility of the Li metal, but still cannot build a stable Li anode for long cycling stability.
Remarkably, in the TME-based LHCE, the Li metal achieved a high initial CE of 93.16% (Fig. 1c), and the CE reached 99.37% after 100 cycles (Fig. 1d).
The corresponding average CE of 120 cycles was 98.87%, even higher than those of the common electrolytes for Li-S batteries with the ­LiNO3 additive.
After adding TME, the LHCE shows an improved CE compared with HCE.
The CE of the battery with LHCE remarkably increased compared with that of LCE.
On the one hand, the total salt concentration of LHCE (1.8 M) is higher than that of LCE (1 M), which could facilitate the formation of a more robust and stable SEI layer.
On the other hand, the local concentration of LHCE is 5.5 M, which is also much higher than that in LCE.
In addition, the CE of LHCE under limited Li was also evaluated.
It can be seen that the CE of Li in LHCE improved to 99.13% with only 4 times excess Li.
When the excess Li was further reduced to 0.5 times, the CE was still 98.35% (Fig.
S2), indicating that a robust SEI is formed on the Li metal anode.
The aggregate capacity loss of Li-Cu batteries was also calculated (Fig. 1e).
An amount of 4 mAh ­cm−2 of Li was deposited on copper foil as the anode and another copper foil as the cathode to assemble a Li-Cu battery.
Under treble of excess Li, the battery with LCE and HCE malfunctioned after 65 and 78 cycles, respectively.
Significantly, after optimizing by diluent TME, the Li-metal battery in the LHCE still worked for over 157 cycles.
Also, the overpotential of Li-Cu with LHCE was much lower thant in other electrolytes and kept stable upon the cycling process (Fig. 1f).

Solvation Structure Analysis of Electrolyte In conventional standard concentration electrolytes, free solvent molecules are sufficient, thus ­Li+ coordinates with the solvent to construct solvent-separated ion pairs (SSIPs).
In HCE and LHCE, most of the anions co-coordinate with
Hou et al. 1 3 ­Li+ to construct contact ion pairs (CIPs) and anion–cation aggregates (AGGs).

The lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) moves from the solvent to the anion and the solvated structure moves from SSIPs in LCE to CIPs and AGGs in HCE and LHCE.32 ­Li+ coordination of SSIPs is relatively loose, and in the CIPs ­(TFSI- coordinated with one ­Li+) and AGGs ­(TFSI- coordinated with two or more ­Li+), the Li ions interact closely with the anions, thus there are extra anions in the ­Li+ solvation ­sheath33 (Fig. 2a).

Since the SEI is generated by competitive breakdown of the solvent and the anions, the LUMO energy level of ­Li+-ether complexes is superior to that of ­Li+-carbonate complexes.34 Accordingly, the anion decomposition in etherbased electrolytes is more pronounced.35 Subsequently, Raman characterization was carried out to investigate the ionic solvation behavior between the three systems (Fig. 2b).
The addition of TME significantly changed the coordination of the Li ions based on the DOL and DME electrolyte systems.
Raman spectra of different electrolytes were obtained.

From LCE to HCE, the characteristic peak of the S-N-S bond gradually shifted from 742 to 746 ­cm−1 (Fig. 2c), corresponding to the transformation of free ­TFSI- in the electrolyte to ­TFSI- coordinated with ­Li+.36 Remarkably, in the TME-based LHCE, the characteristic peak of the S-N-S bond shifted to 749 ­cm–1 (Fig. 2c).
This indicates that ­TFSI- increased in the ­Li+ solvation sheath of LHCE.
Usually, SSIPs in dilute solution occupy the dominant position of a ­Li+ solvation structure.
In highconcentration electrolytes, the structure of CIPs and AGGs gradually increases.
The addition of TME further increases the proportion of the AGGs structure.
There are obvious free solvent characteristic peaks in the DME and DOL solvents, and these peaks still exist in LCE with little offset.

This indicates that, in LCE, most of the DME and DOL remained as free solvent, and most of the coordination structure is SSIPs.
In HCE and LHCE, more DME and DOL coordinate with ­Li+ to form CIPs and AGGs structures.

The addition of TME resulted in a larger proportion of AGGs in LHCE, because it further reduced the free solvent in the ­Li+ solvation sheath.33 Composition of SEI on Li surface As is mentioned above, the Li metal anode in LHCE shows an improved CE compared with LCE and HCE.
Considering that the ionic solvation behavior is closely related to the SEI layer construction, the SEI layer in different electrolytes was studied in detail.
The SEI generated in HCE and LHCE was tested by the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) (Fig. 3).

In the HCE electrolyte, an obvious C-F peak can be seen at the binding energy of 689.1 eV,36 and a relatively weak LiF peak can be seen at 685 eV (Fig. 3a).36 Moreover, there is an obvious ­Li2CO3 peak at 292.6 eV (Fig. 3c).
The main composition of the SEI layer in HCE is a small amount of LiF, ­Li2CO3, and organic oligomer components originated from the sustaining reduction of DOL, such as C-O-C and ­CO2R (Fig. 3c).
As for LHCE, the content of LiF in the SEI is significantly higher than HCE (Fig. 3b), while ­Li2CO3 disappears (Fig. 3d).
The content of ­Li2CO3 is much smaller than that of LiF in LiTFSI-DOL/DME, and the ­Li2CO3 is mostly distributed in the outermost SEI.
Therefore, the content of LiF rises significantly and ­Li2CO3 disappears since the SEI in LHCE is dominated by ­TFSI- decomposition.
This indicates that the addition of TME increased the content of LiF and reduced the proportion of loose ­Li2CO3.
In this case, the anion ­(TFSI-) in LHCE first decomposes to form an SEI dominated by Li salt derivatives.
Outer oligomers (around 286.8 eV) coming from the reduction of DME and DOL were measured (Fig. 3d).

The outer oligomers lead to a more pliable SEI.36,38,39 The dense SEI layer composed of the LiF and the oligomer can impede the formation of Li dendrites, which has good adaptability to the volume expansion during ­Li+ deposition and stripping, thus elevating the cycling performance of Li-S batteries.
Next, we analyzed the effect of TME on the “shuttle effect”.

The fitted peak at the binding energy of 160.2 eV corresponds to the peak of ­Li2S, 40 while the two peaks at the binding energy of 161.6 eV and 162.8 eV correspond to the peak of ­Li2S2.40 For HCE, the content of ­Li2S and ­Li2S2 on the Li surface is very large (Fig. 3e).
After the addition of TME, the content of ­Li2S and ­Li2S2 on the Li surface for LHCE was significantly reduced (Fig. 3f).
Since the reduction of free solvent in the solvated structure inhibited the dissolution of the polysulfides, the “shuttle effect” was suppressed.

The Morphologies of Li Deposition The morphologies were tested by using Li-Cu batteries (Fig. 4 a-f).

The Li-deposition layer in LCE is relatively loose and unevenly distributed, and there are many small debris-like deposits among the Li deposition particles (Fig. 4a, b), which would destroy the cycling reversibility of the Li.
In HCE, the Li deposition morphology is relatively dense, but there are many pores and strip-shaped dendrite protrusions (Fig. 4c, d).
In contrast, the addition TME additives significantly changed the deposition morphology of the Li.
The Li depositions in LHCE were closely packed and uniformly distributed, and Li dendrites can not be observed (Fig. 4e, f).
Combined with the SEI layer composition analysis, the weak Li-ion coordination (SSIPs) in the LCE caused a loose SEI which should be responsible for the unsatisfactory morphology.
In contrast, in HCE, increasing concentration could lead to a more tightly coordinated structure, forming denser SEI, which makes the deposition of Li more uniform and denser than that of LCE.

After the addition of TME, a Li-ion coordination structure dominated by AGGs was formed in the LHCE, forming a more robust SEI than HCE and then facilitating the uniform deposition of Li ions through the most closely coordinated structure.

The EIS results indicted an increased interfacial impedance (RSEI + Rct) during cycling.
The interfacial impedance of Li-Li battery with HCE changed a lot due to the thickened SEI.
Notably, the interfacial impedance of Li-Li battery with LHCE remained stable, which could be attributed to the stable SEI.
Consequently, by combining the modified SEI with the improved solvation structure, a more stable Li metal interface is formed.
After adding the “diluent”, with an external electric field imposed, ­Li+ will move along the cluster including salt and solvent (Fig. 4g).

The Li salt and the diluent are mutually exclusive, so ­Li+ does not move in the diluent.41 The Cycling Performance of Li‐S Batteries First, 50 μL of electrolyte was dropped onto the surface of the separator to observe the wettability of the electrolyte (Fig.
HCE has a high viscosity, cannot spread, and has a large contact angle with the separator.
In comparison, the LHCE obtained by adding the diluent TME has a very low viscosity, spreads out on the separator quickly, and has a smaller contact angle.
At the same time, the electrolyte quickly penetrates the separator and infiltrates the cathode material.
This shows that the addition of the diluent TME can greatly reduce the viscosity without reducing the effective Li salt concentration and increase the wettability.
This promotes ion conduction in Li-S batteries.

The LHCE can keep stable under 4.5 V (Fig.
A Li-S battery was then assembled (Fig. 5a).
The discharge capacity of the battery with HCE continued to decay (Fig. 5b).
The capacity was only left with 463.69 mAh ­g–1 after 400 cycles (Fig.
The capacity retention is just 48.62% (Fig.
S9) and the average CE is only 96.52%.
This is because the higher viscosity and lower ionic conductance affect the utilization of active materials when the concentration is higher.
In contrast, as for the battery with LHCE, the capacity retention is significantly improved (Fig. 5c).
After 400 cycles, the capacity still reaches 554.68 mAh ­g–1 (Fig.
S8), the capacity retention is as high as 60% after 400 cycles (Fig.
S9), and the average CE is 97.73%.

This indicates that with the addition of the diluent TME, the electrolyte has a higher ionic conductivity and lower solubility of polysulfides, which makes the battery with LHCE have a higher active material utilization and capacity retention.
Moreover, the Li metal anode avoids continuous erosion by polysulfides in the presence of a dense SEI layer.
It means that the LiTFSI-DME/DOL-TME system was able to protect Li metal anode and stabilize S cathode.
Conclusions We have successfully prepared a LHCE LiTFSI-DME/DOL- TME which can inhibit the “shuttle effect” of the cathode and build a robust SEI on the anode side to protect the Li metal.
The reduction of free solvent in the Li-ion solvation sheath suppresses the dissolution of polysulfides.
In addition, with increased content of anionic ­TFSI-, Li salt can be preferentially reduced and a LiF-rich SEI layer was achieved.

The obtained Li-Cu battery achieves a low fading rate (the average CE of 98.87% for 120 cycles) and Li-S batteries show high cycling stability (capacity retention rate of 60% after 400 cycles) without the ­LiNO3 additive.
This work gives an approach to construct high-performance Li-S batteries.

Experimental 1.1 Materials Lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI), 1,2-Dimethoxyethane (DME), 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) were bought from the Sigma-Aldrich Corporation. 1,1,2,2-Tetrafluoroethyl methyl ether (TME) was bought from the Aladdin Corporation.
Li foil was purchased from the China Energy Li Corporation.
Copper foil and aluminium foil was obtained from the HF-Kejing Corporation.
For the 1M LiTFSI-DME/DOL electrolyte, 1.0 mmol of LiTFSI was dissolved in 0.5 mL DME and 0.5 mL DOL.
For the 1 LiTFSI-3 DME/DOL electrolyte, 1.0 mmol of LiTFSI was dissolved in 1.5 mmol DME and 1.5 mmol DOL.
For the 1 LiTFSI-3 DME/DOL-6TME electrolyte, additional 6.0 mmol TME was added to 1 LiTFSI-3 DME/DOL electrolyte.
The amount of electrolyte was about 30 μL per battery in Li-S batteries and about 60 μL in other batteries.

The cathode electrode was prepared via mixing S@KB (with 71.2% of sulfur content), Acetylene black (AB) and poly (vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) in N–methylpyrrolidone (NMP) solution, with a mass ratio of 80:10:10.
And then spread the obtained slurry onto a piece of aluminum current collector.
The electrode was then dried under vacuum at 60°C for 24 h.
The mass loading of S was about 0.5 mg cm−2.
Polypropylene (Celgard, 2400) were used as the separators.
Li/Li symmetrical battery was fabricated by using a Li foil as the working electrode, another Li foil as the counter electrode and reference electrode.
Li-Cu batteries was fabricated by using a Li foil as anode, Cu foil as cathode.

Assemble processes were all operated in an argon-filled glove box with oxygen and water contents below 1 ppm. 1.2 Electrochemical measurements Li-Li batteries were used to evaluate the Li deposition and stripping characteristics.
Li-SS batteries were used to evaluate the oxidative stability of the electrolytes.
Li-Cu batteries were used to evaluate the CE of Li metal anode.
The ratio of the charge capacity to the discharge capacity is the CE of the battery.
